Instructions: A specific dosing or PK/PD question is presented. Reason through
(1) the relevant PK/PD index for the drug class (T greater than MIC, AUC/MIC,
Cmax/MIC) and the numeric target for the desired endpoint (stasis, 1-log
kill, clinical cure), (2) how the patient-specific factor (renal function,
obesity, augmented clearance, dialysis) shifts exposure, (3) the recommended
dose adjustment with citation, (4) the toxicity ceiling and how to monitor,
(5) the feedback loop — what TDM target and timing.

PK/PD scenario: Aminoglycoside extended-interval (once-daily) Cmax/MIC target in normal renal function
response:
Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent killers with prominent post-antibiotic
effect (PAE) of 2 to 4 hours; the relevant PK/PD index is Cmax/MIC, with
target Cmax/MIC of 8 to 10 for 1-log kill against gram-negative bacilli
(Moore 1987, J Infect Dis). Extended-interval dosing (Hartford or Hartfordian
regimens, 5 to 7 mg/kg gentamicin once daily, or 15 to 20 mg/kg amikacin
once daily) takes advantage of: (1) Cmax saturation of bacterial 30S
A-site binding; (2) the long PAE that allows interdose drug-free intervals
without losing inhibition; (3) reduced cumulative renal cortical
accumulation, lowering nephrotoxicity from the ~25 percent rate of q8h
dosing to 5 to 8 percent. For target Cmax of 16 to 24 ug/mL gentamicin
(assuming MIC of 2), give 7 mg/kg actual body weight IV over 30 minutes;
check trough at 18 to 22 hours (target less than 1 ug/mL) to confirm
drug clearance before the next dose. Hartford nomogram (Nicolau 1995)
uses the random level at 6 to 14 hours post-dose to set the next interval
(q24, q36, or q48). Patient-specific shift: obesity uses adjusted body
weight (IBW + 0.4*[ABW - IBW]) because aminoglycosides distribute
primarily in lean tissue; pregnancy increases Vd by 30 percent and
requires loading dose adjustment; augmented clearance (CrCl greater than
130, common in young trauma/burn patients) shortens half-life and may
require q12h dosing. Toxicity ceiling: trough greater than 1 (gent) or
greater than 5 (amik) drives nephrotoxicity; cumulative dose greater than
14 days drives ototoxicity (irreversible cochlear damage in 1 to 2
percent). TDM: random or trough level day 2, daily creatinine, audiometry
at baseline and post-treatment for courses over 7 days.

PK/PD scenario: Beta-lactam continuous infusion vs intermittent — fT greater than MIC target in critical illness
response:
Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams) are
time-dependent killers; the PK/PD index is fT greater than MIC (free
drug time above MIC), with class-specific targets: penicillins 50 percent,
cephalosporins 60 to 70 percent, carbapenems 40 percent of dosing
interval. For 1-log kill or critical illness, target greater than 100
percent (Cmin greater than MIC). Continuous infusion (steady-state
concentration constantly above MIC) achieves 100 percent fT greater than
MIC by definition, vs intermittent q6 to q8h that hits 100 percent only
with frequent dosing or low MIC. Patient-specific shift: critical illness
causes augmented renal clearance (hyper-dynamic circulation, fluid
resuscitation increases CrCl to greater than 130 in around 30 percent of
ICU patients per Udy 2014), which shortens beta-lactam half-life and
lowers steady-state concentrations. Hypoalbuminemia (common in critical
illness, albumin less than 25 g/L in 40 percent of ICU patients) raises
free fraction of highly protein-bound beta-lactams (ceftriaxone, ertapenem,
teicoplanin), paradoxically increasing free Cmax but also faster renal
clearance — the net AUC effect is variable. Recommended dose: piperacillin-
tazobactam 4.5 g IV q8h or 12 to 18 g/day continuous infusion;
meropenem 1 g q8h or 4 to 6 g/day continuous; cefepime 2 g q8h or 6 g/day
continuous. Evidence: BLISS RCT (Roberts 2016 CCM) showed continuous
infusion improved clinical cure (56 vs 34 percent) in severe sepsis;
DALI study confirmed PK target attainment doubled with continuous infusion
in ICU. Toxicity: continuous infusion does not raise toxicity thresholds
(carbapenem CNS, cefepime neurotoxicity at high free concentrations); TDM
where available targets free Cmin 4-fold above MIC.

PK/PD scenario: Vancomycin AUC dosing in morbid obesity (BMI greater than 40)
response:
Vancomycin AUC0-24/MIC target is 400 to 600 mg.h/L per 2020 ASHP-IDSA-
PIDS-SIDP consensus update (no longer trough-based). For MRSA bacteremia
with MIC of 1 (broth microdilution), target AUC is 400 (lower bound) to
500 (mid-range); for pneumonia or hVISA suspected, target 600 (upper
bound). Vancomycin distributes primarily in lean body water (Vd ~0.7
L/kg), not adipose; in obesity (BMI greater than 40, weight greater than
120 kg), use ACTUAL body weight for loading dose 25 to 30 mg/kg (cap at
3 g) but adjusted body weight (ABW = IBW + 0.4*[ABW - IBW]) for
maintenance to avoid AUC overshoot. Patient-specific shift: obese patients
have higher CrCl in absolute mL/min terms (kidneys hypertrophy) but
reduced CrCl per kg, leading to overestimation of clearance with
Cockcroft-Gault using actual weight; use lean body weight or
Salazar-Corcoran equation for obesity. Drug-drug consideration: concurrent
piperacillin-tazobactam doubles AKI rate (Hammond 2017 meta), worse in
obese patients with already elevated baseline creatinine. Recommended
approach: 25 to 30 mg/kg actual body weight loading dose (max 3 g over
90 to 120 minutes, slowed for red-man syndrome risk), followed by 15
to 20 mg/kg q8 to 12h based on Bayesian AUC posterior estimate
(single peak at 1 to 2 hours post-infusion + trough before next dose,
around 12 hours post-load). Avoid trough-only monitoring — the
trough-AUC relationship breaks down in obesity. TDM: Bayesian AUC
estimate day 2, daily creatinine, repeat day 5; nephrotoxicity rises
sharply when AUC exceeds 700 (Lodise 2019); switch to alternative
(linezolid, daptomycin, ceftaroline) if AKI develops.

PK/PD scenario: Vancomycin AUC dosing in morbid obesity (BMI greater than 40)

Vancomycin AUC0-24/MIC target is 400 to 600 mg.h/L per 2020 ASHP-IDSA-

PK/PD scenario: Linezolid AUC/MIC and Cmin for mitochondrial toxicity prevention

Linezolid efficacy is AUC/MIC-driven: AUC0-24/MIC greater than 80 to 100

acidosis, peripheral and optic neuropathy) is concentration-dependent

toxicity. TDM: Cmin target less than 7 (preferably less than 5) for

percent drop from baseline triggers reduction or switch); ophthalmology

held. CYP2C19 ultra-rapid metabolizer status alters voriconazole, NOT

PK/PD scenario: Daptomycin high-dose 10 to 12 mg/kg for MRSA bacteremia AUC/MIC bactericidal target
response:
Daptomycin is concentration-dependent with PAE; PK/PD index is AUC/MIC
(Cmax/MIC also correlates), with target AUC0-24/MIC about 666 for 1-log
kill against S. aureus (Safdar 2004). Standard 6 mg/kg q24h IV achieves
AUC ~600 mg.h/L; with MIC of 1, AUC/MIC = 600, marginally below the
bactericidal target. For MRSA bacteremia, IDSA 2011 and updated
guidelines support 8 to 12 mg/kg q24h IV, especially when source-controlled
bacteremia OR vancomycin failure OR MIC creep. At 10 mg/kg, AUC reaches
900 to 1100, comfortably exceeding 666 against MIC 1. Patient-specific
shifts: renal dosing — standard q24h becomes q48h when CrCl less than 30;
hemodialysis — give post-HD on dialysis days; obesity — use ACTUAL body
weight (daptomycin has Vd of 0.1 L/kg, mainly extracellular fluid;
lean-body-weight underdoses obese patients per Pai 2014). Augmented renal
clearance (CrCl greater than 130) may require q12h dosing in young
ICU patients. Toxicity ceiling: the dose-limiting tox is rhabdomyolysis
(CK rise greater than 5x ULN in 1 to 7 percent at 10 to 12 mg/kg vs less
than 1 percent at 6 mg/kg), with risk amplified by concurrent statins
(hold statin during dapto course if possible), renal impairment, or
strenuous exercise. TDM: not routinely available for daptomycin; weekly
CK level, daily creatinine, hold dose if CK greater than 1000 with
muscle symptoms or greater than 2000 asymptomatic. Eosinophilic
pneumonia is a delayed (around week 2 to 4) immunologic toxicity —
not concentration-related but mandates recognition. Pulmonary
contraindication: surfactant inactivates daptomycin in the alveolar
space, making it ineffective for pneumonia regardless of dose.

PK/PD scenario: Voriconazole CYP2C19-genotype-driven dosing and TDM
response:
Voriconazole is metabolized primarily by CYP2C19 (and secondarily by
CYP3A4 and CYP2C9); CYP2C19 has substantial genetic polymorphism that
drives 4-fold inter-individual exposure variability at the same mg/kg
dose. Phenotypes: ultra-rapid metabolizer (UM, *17/*17) — AUC about
0.5x population mean, sub-therapeutic on standard dose; extensive
metabolizer (EM, *1/*1) — population mean exposure; intermediate
metabolizer (IM, *1/*2 or *1/*3) — AUC about 1.5x; poor metabolizer (PM,
*2/*2 or *2/*3) — AUC 2 to 4x. For invasive aspergillosis, the AUC/MIC
target is about 50 (Pascual 2008 CID), and trough levels are the
practical surrogate: target trough 1 to 5.5 ug/mL. Below 1 — risk of
breakthrough infection (UM phenotype patients). Above 5.5 — risk of
hepatotoxicity (4 to 10 percent AST/ALT rise at higher trough), visual
disturbance (photopsia, dose-related retinal A2E rod-cell dysfunction
driven by C-19 retinal effect), encephalopathy in elderly. CPIC
pharmacogenomics guideline (Moriyama 2017) recommends pre-emptive
genotyping and dose adjustment: UM/EM standard 6 mg/kg load q12h x 24h
then 4 mg/kg q12h IV (or 200 mg PO BID); IM/PM start at 50 to 75
percent of standard. Even with genotyping, trough TDM is essential at
day 5 to 7 (steady state) and weekly thereafter; switch to
isavuconazole (linear PK, no TDM required) if voriconazole levels
cannot be reliably attained. Drug-drug: voriconazole inhibits CYP3A4,
raising tacrolimus, sirolimus, cyclosporine levels in transplant
patients (reduce dose to 1/3 and TDM the partner drug).

PK/PD scenario: Posaconazole DR-tablet vs oral suspension absorption and Cmin target in mucormycosis
response:
Posaconazole is the first-line triazole for invasive mucormycosis
(Rhizopus, Mucor) where voriconazole has NO activity. The PK/PD target
is Cmin (trough) greater than 1.25 ug/mL for mucormycosis treatment
(Cornely 2014 ECMM/ESCMID guideline) and greater than 0.7 for prophylaxis
in AML/SCT. Oral suspension formulation has erratic absorption (highly
food-dependent — without high-fat meal, bioavailability drops to 10
percent; with cola pH 2.5 and high-fat meal, around 50 percent), making
it unreliable for mucormycosis where consistent target attainment is
life-or-death. Delayed-release tablet (DR-tab) and IV solution were
developed to overcome this: DR-tab gives reliable bioavailability
~50 percent independent of food, and IV (cyclodextrin-vehicle) gives
direct AUC delivery. Dosing: DR-tab 300 mg PO q12h x 1 day load, then
300 mg PO daily; IV 300 mg IV q12h x 1 day load, then 300 mg daily.
Patient-specific shifts: severe mucositis or vomiting in stem-cell
transplant patients requires IV (oral absorption fails); renal
failure of CrCl less than 50 — avoid IV (cyclodextrin vehicle
accumulates and causes renal tubular damage), use DR-tab; hepatic
impairment — TDM-guided dose reduction. TDM: posaconazole trough
day 5 to 7 then weekly, target greater than 1.25 ug/mL for treatment;
adjust dose by 25 to 50 percent if outside range. Toxicity: hepatic
enzyme rise (5 to 12 percent), QTc prolongation, mineralocorticoid-like
effect (11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase inhibition causes
hypokalemia, hypertension, edema — most prominent at trough greater
than 4); monitor K, BP, ECG. Switch to isavuconazole if posaconazole
cannot be attained or tox limits use.

PK/PD scenario: Cefiderocol fT greater than MIC 75 percent with extended 3-h infusion in CRAB
response:
Cefiderocol is a siderophore-cephalosporin with PK/PD index fT greater
than MIC; the target for stasis is 75 percent of dosing interval (higher
than typical cephalosporins because of competitive iron uptake and
siderophore-receptor saturation effects per Yamano 2019). Standard dose
is 2 g IV q8h infused over 3 hours (extended infusion to maximize T
greater than MIC) for normal CrCl 60 to 119; 1.5 g q8h for CrCl 30 to
60; 1 g q8h for CrCl 15 to 30; 0.75 g q12h for CrCl less than 15;
and 2 g q6h for augmented clearance (CrCl greater than 120 — common in
ICU/burn patients). Pathogen MIC50 against CRAB (carbapenem-resistant
A. baumannii) is 1 to 4 ug/mL, against NDM/VIM Pseudomonas 1 to 2,
against KPC-CRE 0.5 to 1; serum free concentrations at standard dose
reach 30 to 50 ug/mL Cmax with 3-hour infusion, giving 75 percent fT
greater than MIC for all clinically targeted gram-negatives. Resistance
emergence: cirA (siderophore-receptor) mutations reduce uptake and shift
MIC to 8 to 32 — molecular surveillance recommended for CRAB outbreaks.
Patient shift: liver failure does not require dose change (renal
clearance dominant); ICU augmented clearance may cause underdosing
with q8h — switch to q6h or 4 g/day continuous infusion in select
cases. Toxicity ceiling: well-tolerated; main adverse effects are
diarrhea (8 percent), hepatic enzyme rise (3 percent), QTc prolongation
(modest, 5 to 8 ms), CRAB CREDIBLE-CR trial showed numerically higher
mortality vs best-available therapy in CRAB pneumonia (FDA black-box
consideration), although attribution is debated. TDM not standard;
MIC of clinical isolate is the operative metric.

PK/PD scenario: Tigecycline AUC/MIC failure in bacteremia — Cmax 0.6 ug/mL ceiling
response:
Tigecycline PK/PD index is AUC0-24/MIC, target around 17 for stasis
against gram-negatives and around 7 for gram-positives (Rubino 2010).
Standard dose is 100 mg IV load then 50 mg q12h, achieving steady-state
Cmax of 0.6 ug/mL and AUC0-24 of 5 to 6 mg.h/L. Against MRSA with MIC
of 0.25, AUC/MIC is 24 — adequate. Against ESBL E. coli with MIC of
0.5, AUC/MIC is 12 — marginal. Against Acinetobacter or Stenotrophomonas
with MIC of 1 to 2, AUC/MIC is 3 to 6 — sub-therapeutic. The Cmax
ceiling around 0.6 ug/mL is the fundamental PK problem: tigecycline
distributes extensively into tissues (Vd 7 to 10 L/kg, lung-tissue
to plasma ratio about 8) but plasma free concentration plateaus at sub-MIC
for most gram-negatives. In bacteremia, where clearance of bloodstream
organisms requires sustained free drug above MIC, tigecycline fails
consistently — FDA 2010 black-box warning issued because pooled
meta-analysis of 13 RCTs showed 0.6 percent absolute mortality
increase in tigecycline arms, driven by bacteremia trials. Recommended
dose escalation: high-dose tigecycline 100 mg q12h (double-dose) raises
AUC to 10 to 12 mg.h/L and improves AUC/MIC for Acinetobacter; supported
by Falagas 2014 retrospective and used clinically in CRAB despite no
registration. Patient shift: hepatic failure (Child-Pugh C) reduces
glucuronidation clearance, lower dose 25 mg q12h after initial load.
Renal failure no adjustment needed (biliary excretion dominant). TDM
not clinical practice; better answer is to use tigecycline only for
cSSSI and complicated intra-abdominal where local tissue concentrations
compensate, NOT for bacteremia. Eravacycline addresses the Cmax limit
partially (twice tigecycline's Cmax at 1.0 mg/kg q12h IV).

PK/PD scenario: Caspofungin in moderate hepatic impairment Child-Pugh B — dose reduction
response:
Caspofungin clearance is hepatic (degradation by N-acetylation and
hydrolysis to peptide products, then biliary excretion); the PK/PD
index is AUC/MIC, target around 250 for stasis against Candida (Andes
2010, AAC). Standard dose is 70 mg IV load x 1 then 50 mg IV q24h.

B (moderate) — give 70 mg load then 35 mg q24h (50 percent reduction)
because clearance drops about 30 percent and AUC rises proportionally;
the rationale is to maintain target AUC without overshoot toward
hepatotoxicity. Child-Pugh C (severe) — limited data; consider
micafungin or anidulafungin (less hepatic-dependent). Patient shifts:
cyclosporine increases caspofungin AUC by 35 percent (transient hepatic
enzyme rise reported); rifampin/dexamethasone induce caspofungin
clearance (raise dose to 70 mg q24h). Pediatric: weight-based 50
mg/m^2 daily after 70 mg/m^2 load (max 70 mg). For CNS candidiasis,

routine; clinical response and serial blood cultures are the operative
surrogates. FKS mutation surveillance is the molecular feedback loop
replacing TDM in the echinocandin class.

(2) what major pathogens it does NOT cover and the named structural reason,
(3) the typical clinical positioning and the rationale (why prefer over

Drug spectrum: Doxycycline — broad gram-positive, atypical, vector-borne coverage
response:
Coverage: gram-positive (S. aureus including community MRSA, S. pneumoniae,
group A and B streptococci), atypicals (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia
pneumoniae and trachomatis, Legionella pneumophila), vector-borne pathogens
(Borrelia burgdorferi/Lyme, Rickettsia rickettsii/Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever,
Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Ehrlichia chaffeensis, Coxiella burnetii/Q fever,
Rickettsia prowazekii/typhus), some gram-negatives (Vibrio cholerae,
Yersinia pestis, Francisella tularensis/tularemia, Brucella, Bartonella),
and protozoa (Plasmodium prophylaxis, Balantidium). Mechanistic feature:
doxycycline binds 30S ribosomal A-site at h34 of 16S rRNA; the
C7 dimethylamino group, C5 hydroxyl, and 6-alpha-deoxy modification give
lipophilicity that drives intracellular concentration (essential for
Rickettsia, Anaplasma, Chlamydia which are obligate intracellular). NOT
covered: enterococci (intrinsic ribosomal protection in gram-positive
cocci? more accurately, marginal MIC); Pseudomonas (intrinsic outer-
membrane impermeability and MexAB-OprM efflux); B. fragilis and most
anaerobes (variable, with some tet-gene-positive strains resistant);
MRSA in hospital-acquired strains often carrying tetK/tetM. Clinical
positioning: tick-borne disease (Lyme, RMSF, anaplasmosis) is doxycycline-
first because of intracellular activity unique to tetracyclines; community-
acquired pneumonia (CAP) outpatient atypical coverage when macrolide
resistance exceeds 25 percent (which is typical in 2024 US S. pneumoniae);
malaria prophylaxis. Resistance: tet(M) ribosomal protection and tet(K)
efflux raise MIC 4 to 16-fold. Stewardship: prefer over levofloxacin in
atypical CAP for tendinopathy/QTc/C diff sparing; prefer over azithromycin
for atypical pneumonia in regions with high pneumococcal macrolide
resistance; ALWAYS use over oral cephalosporin or amoxicillin-clavulanate
for suspected tick-borne disease.

Drug spectrum: Clindamycin — anaerobes, gram-positive, antitoxin
response:
Coverage: streptococci (S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae, S. pneumoniae if
D-test negative), MSSA and community MRSA (D-test negative; D-test
positive isolates have inducible MLSb resistance), most anaerobes
(Bacteroides fragilis when not tet-positive, Prevotella, Fusobacterium,
Peptostreptococcus, Clostridium perfringens), atypicals partially (none
reliably), protozoa Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium and Babesia
(synergy with primaquine for PCP, with quinine for babesiosis,
with pyrimethamine for toxo). Mechanistic feature: binds 50S ribosome
at A2058 and U2611 of 23S rRNA, blocking peptide bond formation; same
binding site as macrolides explains MLSb cross-resistance. The "anti-toxin"
property unique to clindamycin: independent of bacterial growth,
clindamycin halts ribosomal synthesis of streptococcal toxins (M-protein,
streptolysin) and staphylococcal exotoxins (TSST-1, alpha-hemolysin),
providing critical adjunct in necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock
syndrome — beta-lactams do NOT inhibit toxin production at sub-MIC.
NOT covered: Enterococcus (intrinsic, low ribosomal affinity), all
gram-negative aerobes (intrinsic, OM impermeability), Mycoplasma (50S
mutation), MAC, Legionella. Clinical positioning: necrotizing fasciitis
add-on with penicillin or vancomycin (Eagle effect — clindamycin
remains active in stationary phase when beta-lactams fail); CA-MRSA
SSTI (when D-test negative); Toxoplasma encephalitis in HIV; intra-abdominal
anaerobic coverage when metronidazole alternatives needed. Resistance:
Erm methylation of A2058 (constitutive or inducible MLSb); D-test
mandatory before use in S. aureus. Stewardship: AVOID monotherapy if
D-test inducible (selects constitutive MLSb mutants); HIGH C. difficile
risk (relative risk 15 to 20-fold) — keep courses short and monitor;
not first-line for CDI-prone elderly.

Drug spectrum: Linezolid — universal gram-positive plus M. tuberculosis
response:
Coverage: ALL clinically significant gram-positive bacteria — MRSA, VRE
(faecium and faecalis), all streptococci, Listeria, Corynebacterium
jeikeium, Nocardia (variable), M. tuberculosis (XDR-TB regimen component
in BPaL/BPaLM), M. avium and M. abscessus (limited). Mechanistic feature:
binds 50S A-site at A2451 of 23S rRNA, blocking 70S initiation complex
formation — a mechanism distinct from macrolides, lincosamides,
streptogramin (no cross-resistance via MLSb). The (S)-acetamidomethyl
group at C5 of the oxazolidinone is the universal binding handle (do
not modify); the morpholine D-ring of linezolid (or the
pyridinyl-pyrimidinyl of tedizolid) defines class members. NOT covered:
gram-negative aerobes (intrinsic — efflux via AcrAB-TolC keeps internal
concentrations sub-MIC), most anaerobes (variable; B. fragilis MIC
4 to 16). Clinical positioning: VRE bacteremia (alternative to dapto
and the ONLY drug with consistent oral bioavailability for chronic
VRE infection); MRSA pneumonia (ZEPHyR trial, Wunderink 2012, showed
clinical-cure benefit over vancomycin for HAP/VAP MRSA — superior
epithelial-lining-fluid penetration); MDR-TB and XDR-TB long-course
therapy (BPaL); hospital outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy
(OPAT) where oral switch is desirable. Resistance: cfr methyltransferase
(transmissible plasmid) methylates A2503, raising MIC to 8 to 16,
conferring cross-resistance to chloramphenicol AND lefamulin (PhLOPSa
phenotype: phenicol, linc, oxa, pleuro, strepto-A); 23S rRNA G2576T
mutations are chromosomal and require multiple alleles for high-level
resistance. Stewardship: short-course preferred (less than 14 days)
because of mitochondrial protein synthesis inhibition driving
thrombocytopenia (~30 percent at 14 days), peripheral and optic
neuropathy (greater than 28 days), lactic acidosis. Hold SSRIs (MAO-A
inhibition by linezolid → serotonin syndrome). Tedizolid 200 mg daily
is a once-daily, lower-tox alternative with same spectrum.

Drug spectrum: Tigecycline — broad MRSA/VRE/ESBL/anaerobe spectrum, NO Pseudomonas
response:
Coverage: MRSA, VRE faecium and faecalis, S. pneumoniae (penicillin-R
and macrolide-R), enterococci, ESBL Enterobacterales (E. coli, K. pneumoniae,
Enterobacter), KPC-CRE (resistance limited by AdeABC overexpression in
Acinetobacter), most anaerobes (B. fragilis, Prevotella, Fusobacterium),
atypicals (Legionella, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae), Mycobacterium
abscessus and M. fortuitum, Stenotrophomonas (alternative). Mechanistic
feature: 30S A-site binding via tetracycline core; the bulky C9 t-butyl-
glycylamido side chain prevents TetA-class efflux pump recognition AND
Tet(M) ribosomal protection access — escape from the dominant tet-resistance
mechanisms. The C7 dimethylamino retained from minocycline gives
lipophilicity and intracellular concentration. NOT covered: P. aeruginosa
(intrinsic — MexXY-OprM efflux pumps export tigecycline; outer membrane
permeability also limits), Proteus, Providencia, Morganella (intrinsic
tet-A-like efflux). Clinical positioning: complicated intra-abdominal
infection (cIAI) with anaerobic and ESBL coverage in single agent;
complicated SSTI with MRSA/VRE concerns; salvage in CRAB or
Stenotrophomonas. Resistance: tetX FAD-monooxygenase (hydroxylates
C11a) emerging in Enterobacterales raises MIC to 4 to 8; AdeABC
overexpression in Acinetobacter raises MIC. Pharmacology constraint:
Cmax ceiling around 0.6 ug/mL drives AUC/MIC failure in BACTEREMIA,
leading to FDA mortality black-box (Tigecycline FDA 2010); positioning
restricted to non-bacteremic indications. Stewardship: AVOID for
bacteremia, ventilator-associated pneumonia (HAP/VAP — no anti-Pseudomonas
coverage), or where Cmax/MIC matters. Use as definitive therapy ONLY
with susceptibility-confirmed isolate and tissue/intra-abdominal
indication where local tissue concentrations compensate.

Drug spectrum: Ceftaroline — anti-MRSA cephalosporin without enterococcal or Pseudomonas activity
response:
Coverage: MRSA (the unique selling point — MIC50 1 ug/mL via PBP2a
allosteric binding), MSSA, all streptococci including penicillin-resistant
S. pneumoniae, Listeria (limited), Hemophilus, Moraxella, ESBL-naive
Enterobacterales (E. coli, K. pneumoniae, Proteus), AmpC-derepressed
Enterobacter (modestly), some anaerobes (S. anginosus group). Mechanistic
feature: C3 thiazolyl-pyridinium with phosphono-prodrug (ceftaroline fosamil)
reaches PBP2a's allosteric site at residue Glu447 region, triggering
conformational opening of the active-site groove that excludes other
cephalosporins; the C7 aminothiazole-oxime is preserved for gram-negative
activity. Adds anti-MRSA activity to a 3G-class cephalosporin scaffold —
first-in-class. NOT covered: Pseudomonas (intrinsic — no penetration past
OprD porin, MexAB-OprM efflux), Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas, ESBL
producers (CTX-M-15 hydrolyzes ceftaroline at standard concentrations),
enterococci (intrinsic low affinity at PBP5 of E. faecium), most anaerobes
including B. fragilis. Clinical positioning: community-acquired pneumonia
(CABP) when MRSA suspected; complicated SSTI with MRSA/MSSA/streptococci;
add-on for MRSA bacteremia (combination with vancomycin or daptomycin —
"see-saw effect" where ceftaroline alters membrane charge and restores
dapto sensitivity). Resistance: PBP2a mutations near allosteric site
(Glu447Lys, Tyr446Asn) raise MIC; ESBL hydrolysis defeats it. Stewardship:
NOT empirical for HAP/VAP without anti-Pseudomonas partner; not appropriate
for ESBL-suspected bacteremia (use carbapenem); useful as MRSA-targeted
cephalosporin in specific bacteremia and pneumonia scenarios.

Drug spectrum: Cefiderocol — universal gram-negative including MBL, no gram-positive coverage

Drug spectrum: Aztreonam — gram-negative-only monobactam, MBL-stable
response:
Coverage: aerobic gram-negatives — Enterobacterales (E. coli, Klebsiella,
Proteus, Salmonella), P. aeruginosa, Hemophilus, Neisseria; some
partial activity against Acinetobacter. Mechanistic feature: monobactam
structure (single beta-lactam ring without the fused thiazolidine of
penicillins or dihydrothiazine of cephalosporins); binds PBP3 of
gram-negatives selectively. The monobactam scaffold is intrinsically
stable against class B metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP) because
the Zn coordination chemistry of MBLs requires bicyclic beta-lactam
ring orientation that is absent from monobactams — aztreonam is the
ONLY beta-lactam with reliable MBL stability. NOT covered: gram-positive
bacteria (intrinsic — no PBP affinity in gram-positives), anaerobes,
Bacteroides, intracellular pathogens. Vulnerable to class A ESBL (CTX-M,
TEM, SHV) and class C AmpC; therefore requires partner BLI (avibactam,
sulbactam-durlobactam) when these enzymes co-exist with MBL.
Aztreonam-avibactam is the combination drug — avibactam protects aztreonam
from CTX-M and AmpC while aztreonam itself remains MBL-stable, giving
activity against the difficult NDM-positive ESBL co-producers. Clinical
positioning: penicillin-allergic patients needing gram-negative coverage
(no cross-reactivity with penicillin allergens because monobactam ring
lacks penicillin's bicyclic structure); MBL-producing CRE bacteremia
via aztreonam-avibactam combination. Resistance: ESBL hydrolysis (defeated
by avibactam combination), PBP3 mutations, oprD-loss in Pseudomonas.
Stewardship: aztreonam monotherapy useful in pen-allergic patient with
susceptible Enterobacterales or Pseudomonas; aztreonam-avibactam reserved
for documented MBL-producing isolate; AVOID in S. aureus or
enterococcal indications.

Drug spectrum: Meropenem-vaborbactam — KPC focus, NOT MBL
response:
Coverage: KPC-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE),
class A serine carbapenemases (KPC-2, KPC-3, KPC-31), all the
meropenem-susceptible bacteria (Enterobacterales, P. aeruginosa,
Acinetobacter MIC-dependent, MSSA, S. pneumoniae, anaerobes including
B. fragilis, Listeria). Mechanistic feature: meropenem provides the
antibiotic backbone with carbapenem potency and DHP-1 stability via
1-beta-methyl. Vaborbactam is a cyclic boronic-acid-class beta-lactamase
inhibitor with reversible covalent binding to class A serine
beta-lactamases via Ser-O-B(OH)2 tetrahedral intermediate (the boron
mimics tetrahedral transition state of beta-lactam hydrolysis). Vaborbactam
restores meropenem MIC against KPC-producing K. pneumoniae from greater
than 64 to 0.06 to 1 (Lomovskaya 2017 AAC). NOT covered: MBL producers
(NDM, VIM, IMP — vaborbactam is class A serine specific, no MBL coverage;
meropenem alone is hydrolyzed by MBL); OXA-48 (poor inhibition by
vaborbactam); Stenotrophomonas (intrinsic L1 MBL); B. fragilis with
cfiA gene. Clinical positioning: KPC-CRE bacteremia, complicated UTI,
pyelonephritis, complicated intra-abdominal infection — TANGO-II trial
(Wunderink 2018) showed superior cure vs best-available therapy in
KPC-CRE infections. Resistance: KPC mutations (KPC-31 D179Y) confer
resistance to ceftaz-avi but PRESERVE meropenem-vaborbactam activity —
the two drugs are complementary in the KPC-CRE armamentarium. Porin
loss (OmpK35/OmpK36) in K. pneumoniae raises MIC; carrying both KPC
and OmpK loss may shift MIC to greater than 8. Stewardship: confirmation
of KPC carbapenemase before use; avoid for empirical coverage; prefer
mero-vab over ceftaz-avi when KPC-31-type escape mutation is present;
switch to cefiderocol or aztreonam-avibactam if MBL is documented.

Drug spectrum: Rifaximin — gut-restricted, hepatic encephalopathy / IBS-D / traveler
response:
Coverage: gram-positive and gram-negative gut bacteria, especially
Enterobacterales (E. coli including ETEC strains causing traveler's
diarrhea), Bacteroides, Clostridium (NOT C. difficile reliably; some
activity against vegetative C. difficile but NOT spores); reduces gut
ammonia-producing bacteria contributing to hepatic encephalopathy.
Mechanistic feature: rifaximin is a non-systemically-absorbed rifamycin
derivative with a pyrido-imidazo modification that confers gut-restricted
pharmacology — oral bioavailability is less than 0.4 percent, so almost
all administered drug remains in the gastrointestinal lumen. Mechanism:
binds bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase beta subunit (rpoB), inhibiting
transcription, same as systemic rifampin. Because rifaximin does not
enter systemic circulation, it spares gut microbiome only in the lumen,
and bacterial rpoB exposure does NOT drive systemic resistance to
rifampin (a critical practical advantage). NOT covered: bacteremia
(rifaximin does not reach bloodstream), CNS infection, urinary infection;
no useful spectrum outside the gut lumen. Clinical positioning: travelers'
diarrhea (E. coli ETEC, Shigella, Campylobacter) — 200 mg PO TID x 3
days; hepatic encephalopathy prevention/treatment in cirrhosis (550 mg
PO BID; reduces overt HE recurrence by 58 percent per Bass 2010 NEJM);
irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea (IBS-D) — 550 mg PO TID x 14 days
(Pimentel 2011 NEJM showed symptomatic benefit). Resistance: rpoB
mutations emerge with prolonged use; no clinically significant
cross-resistance to systemic rifampin observed in clinical M. tuberculosis
isolates because of the pharmacological compartment separation.
Stewardship: avoid for systemic infection (cannot reach target); avoid
for C. difficile prophylaxis (no proven benefit; metronidazole or
vancomycin oral are the agents); short-course traveler's diarrhea is
well-tolerated; long-course cirrhosis use requires LFT monitoring.

Drug spectrum: Aztreonam-avibactam — MBL-positive Enterobacterales when ESBL co-exists
response:
Coverage: gram-negative bacteria producing METALLO-beta-lactamases
(NDM-1/-2/-7, VIM-1/-2/-4, IMP-1/-4) co-existing with class A ESBLs
(CTX-M-15, TEM, SHV) and class C AmpC; the 1-2-punch combination that
addresses the multi-class enzyme repertoire of contemporary CRE.
Mechanistic feature: aztreonam (monobactam) is intrinsically stable to
MBL hydrolysis (class B Zn-mediated chemistry cannot orient the
monobactam ring for hydrolysis) but is hydrolyzed by class A ESBL and
class C AmpC. Avibactam (DBO inhibitor with bridgehead 2-OH) covalently
acylates Ser70 of class A and class C beta-lactamases with carbamoyl
acyl-enzyme that recyclizes (slow off-rate, sustained inhibition over
hours). The combination protects aztreonam from ESBL/AmpC hydrolysis
while aztreonam itself defeats MBL via inherent stability. Result:
activity against NDM-positive K. pneumoniae and E. coli that also carry
CTX-M-15 (the dominant clinical phenotype globally — NDM rarely occurs
alone; it sits on plasmids carrying CTX-M and other resistance genes).
NOT covered: gram-positive (no PBP-3 affinity in gram-positive
monobactam-target), enterococci, MRSA, S. pneumoniae, anaerobes
including B. fragilis. Pseudomonas with VIM only (where aztreonam-avibactam
retains activity); Stenotrophomonas (intrinsic L1 MBL — but L2 ESBL is
avibactam-inhibited, so partial activity exists for some isolates).
Clinical positioning: pivotal phase 3 REVISIT and ASSEMBLE trials showed
activity against MBL-CRE; FDA approved 2024 (or imminent depending on
timeline) for cIAI, cUTI, HAP/VAP from MBL-producing Enterobacterales;
reserved as last-line. Resistance: NDM-7 with PBP3 inserts is emerging
as escape mutation; cefiderocol is alternative. Stewardship: confirm
NDM/VIM/IMP molecular detection (NG-Test CARBA-5, blaNDM/blaVIM PCR)
before use; avoid empirical first-line; partner with infection control
to limit MBL-CRE spread.

Instructions: An empirical-therapy or de-escalation decision is presented.
Reason through (1) what the local epidemiology and prior cultures imply about
resistance probability, (2) which drug to choose or de-escalate to and why,
(3) the duration appropriate for this syndrome with citation to landmark
duration trials, (4) collateral damage to consider (C. difficile, ESBL induction,
AKI), (5) what the next decision point is and what data triggers it.

Stewardship case: 5-day vs 10-day uncomplicated cellulitis — Hepburn 2004 short-course
response:
45-year-old with non-purulent cellulitis of the lower leg, no abscess,
no systemic toxicity, no diabetes, no bite wound, no immune compromise.
Most cases are caused by group A Streptococcus or beta-hemolytic
streptococci (S. agalactiae, S. dysgalactiae); MSSA accounts for a
minority of non-purulent cellulitis. Empirical first-line: cephalexin
500 mg PO QID OR penicillin VK 500 mg PO QID; if MRSA risk (prior
MRSA, IV drug use, recurrent SSTI), add doxycycline 100 mg BID or
TMP-SMX. Duration: Hepburn 2004 (Arch Intern Med, NEJM) randomized
trial showed 5-day course non-inferior to 10-day for clinical cure
(98 vs 98 percent). IDSA 2014 SSTI guideline endorses 5 days for
uncomplicated cellulitis. Stewardship move: 5-day course (cephalexin
500 mg QID x 5 days), reassess at 48 to 72 hours; extend only if
slow response. Avoid: routine 10-day or 14-day courses (no benefit,
excess C. difficile risk and collateral); empirical IV vancomycin
(oral options work for non-purulent cellulitis); coverage for
Pseudomonas (not the typical cellulitis pathogen). Next decision:
48-hour assessment — improving redness/edema, pain, fever; if
worsening, image to rule out abscess (drainage required) or
necrotizing fasciitis (surgical emergency, broad coverage with
vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin for toxin
suppression).

Stewardship case: Discontinue empirical vancomycin at 48h with MRSA nasal PCR negative for HAP
response:
ICU patient with hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) day 4 of admission;
empirical regimen started with vancomycin (15 mg/kg q12h) plus
piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g q6h, extended infusion) for broad
MRSA + Pseudomonas coverage. MRSA nasal PCR returns negative at 24
hours; sputum culture growing only Klebsiella pneumoniae sensitive to
pip-tazo. Stewardship move: discontinue vancomycin at 48 hours.
Rationale: MRSA nasal PCR has a high negative predictive value (around
99 percent) for excluding MRSA pneumonia (Parente 2018, CID; Carr 2018,
Open Forum Infect Dis); when combined with negative sputum culture
growth at 48 hours, the probability of MRSA pneumonia drops below 1
percent, making continued vancomycin futile and harmful. Collateral
damage avoided: vancomycin AKI rate ~16 percent at AUC greater than
600, especially when paired with piperacillin-tazobactam (Hammond 2017
meta showed doubling of AKI rate with the combination); preserves

Stewardship case: Avoid empirical antibiotics in viral pharyngitis with Centor 0 to 1
response:
28-year-old presents with sore throat, mild fever 37.8C, cough,
rhinorrhea, no exudate, no tender anterior cervical adenopathy. Centor
score 0 (no fever greater than 38, no exudate, no anterior LAD, has
cough); modified Centor (McIsaac) similarly low. Probability of group
A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis in this clinical picture is less
than 5 percent — most cases are viral (rhinovirus, adenovirus, EBV,
enterovirus). Stewardship move: do NOT prescribe antibiotics; supportive
care (acetaminophen, fluids, salt-water gargle, lozenges); reserve
rapid-strep test and culture for higher Centor scores (3 to 4).
Rationale: empirical antibiotics in viral pharyngitis offer no
symptom benefit (Spurling 2017 Cochrane); drive C. difficile risk
(8.5x in 90 days post-exposure to even short courses);
drive S. pyogenes resistance (macrolide resistance has risen to 15
to 25 percent in some US regions due to outpatient overuse); add
anaphylaxis and SJS risk; cost. IDSA 2012 GAS pharyngitis guideline:
penicillin VK 500 mg PO BID or QID x 10 days, OR amoxicillin 1 g daily
x 10 days, OR cephalexin (penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis) ONLY
if rapid-strep positive or culture-confirmed GAS. Avoid azithromycin
first-line (resistance rising). Next decision: if symptoms persist
beyond 5 days, worsen, or develop scarlet-fever-like rash or peritonsillar
abscess, reassess and test; if mononucleosis features (lymphadenopathy,
splenomegaly), monospot or EBV serology — and AVOID amoxicillin in
EBV (causes morbilliform rash in 90 percent).

Stewardship case: IV-to-PO switch fluoroquinolone or beta-lactam at clinical stability
response:
62-year-old hospitalized with pyelonephritis, started on IV
ceftriaxone 1 g q24h. Day 2 — afebrile, hemodynamically stable,
tolerating diet, blood cultures negative, urine culture growing
ceftriaxone-S E. coli, creatinine improving. Stewardship move:
switch IV ceftriaxone to oral cefpodoxime 200 mg q12h or
ciprofloxacin 500 mg q12h or amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg
q12h (susceptibility-guided) at clinical stability. Rationale: oral
switch criteria (the COMS criteria of Cunha 2008): (C) Clinical
improvement, (O) Oral route works (no ileus, no NPO, no severe
vomiting), (M) Markers improving (fever, WBC trending down,
hemodynamic stability), (S) Susceptibility-guided drug. IDSA 2010
complicated UTI/pyelonephritis guideline supports IV-to-PO switch
typically within 48 to 72 hours of fever resolution. Total duration
7 days for uncomplicated pyelonephritis (cipro or fluoroquinolone) or
10 to 14 days for beta-lactam (Sandberg 2012 Lancet trial showed
7-day cipro non-inferior to 14-day for women with pyelonephritis).
Stewardship benefit: shorter LOS, lower cost, lower line-related
bacteremia risk, lower nosocomial pathogen acquisition. Avoid:
empirical IV continuation just because patient remains hospitalized
for other reasons; nephrotoxic IV antibiotics when oral options work.
Next decision: 24-hour post-PO-switch reassessment — if symptoms
worsen on oral, exclude obstruction (renal ultrasound for
hydronephrosis, cyst); if cultures show resistance, switch
empirical class.

Stewardship case: Avoid antibiotics for asymptomatic candiduria
response:
78-year-old in long-term care with indwelling urinary catheter; routine
urinalysis pre-procedure shows pyuria; urine culture grows greater
than 10^5 CFU/mL Candida albicans. Patient afebrile, no flank pain,
no urinary symptoms attributable to UTI, no immunosuppression, no
planned urological procedure with mucosal trauma. Stewardship move:
do NOT treat. Remove the catheter if no longer indicated (most
catheter-associated candiduria resolves with catheter removal).
Repeat urine culture after catheter removal is NOT routinely
indicated. IDSA 2016 candidiasis guideline: asymptomatic candiduria
should NOT be treated in non-pregnant adults regardless of
pyuria, regardless of catheter status, EXCEPT in three scenarios:
(1) neutropenic patients (treat as candidemia source); (2) very
low birth weight neonates; (3) patients undergoing urological
manipulation with mucosal trauma (peri-procedural fluconazole
400 mg PO daily x 1 day before to several days after). Rationale
for non-treatment: candiduria represents colonization in most
cases, not infection; treatment with fluconazole drives selection
for fluconazole-resistant Candida glabrata and C. krusei;
antifungals add hepatic enzyme rise, QTc prolongation, drug-drug
interactions; no evidence treatment improves outcomes (Sobel 2000
retrospective, no benefit). Avoid: amphotericin bladder irrigation
(no benefit for invasive disease, has not shown long-term clearance);
reflexive systemic antifungal based on lab finding alone. Next
decision: treat ONLY if true candidemia (positive blood culture)
OR symptomatic candidiasis (cystitis with delirium attributed to
UTI in elderly with sterile blood-pus workup); fluconazole 200
to 400 mg daily x 14 days for documented true infection.

Stewardship case: Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic stop in suspected bacterial pneumonia
response:
ICU patient with possible HAP — fever, rising WBC, infiltrate on
chest X-ray; empirical pip-tazo started. Initial procalcitonin (PCT)
0.4 ng/mL (low-positive); blood cultures and respiratory cultures
pending. Day 3 PCT drops to 0.15 ng/mL with clinical improvement;
cultures negative. Stewardship move: stop empirical antibiotics at
day 3 because of low and falling PCT plus negative cultures and
improving clinical course. Rationale: PCT-guided algorithms (de Jong
2016 Lancet ID, SAPS trial) showed that stopping antibiotics when
PCT drops greater than 80 percent from peak OR falls below 0.5 ng/mL
reduces antibiotic days by 1.2 days without affecting mortality (in
fact, lower 1-year mortality observed in the de-escalation arm).
For severe sepsis/septic shock in ICU, PROGRESS and PRORATA trials
similarly support PCT-guided cessation. Caveat: PCT has lower
sensitivity in localized infections (intra-abdominal, hardware-
associated, biliary), so do not rely on PCT alone in those scenarios.
Stewardship benefit: shorter antibiotic days reduce C. difficile risk
(every additional day raises CDI risk by 8 to 12 percent), reduce
antimicrobial resistance pressure, reduce drug-related toxicity
(AKI, encephalopathy). Avoid: continuing antibiotics "just because"
patient is in ICU with uncertain diagnosis; chasing radiographic
infiltrates that do not represent active infection (atelectasis,
ARDS, pulmonary hemorrhage). Next decision: if clinical worsening
occurs after stopping, repeat cultures, repeat imaging, restart
empirical broad-spectrum based on hospital antibiogram for HAP risk
factors; otherwise complete supportive care without antibiotics.

Stewardship case: OPAT eligibility for outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy
response:
55-year-old completing inpatient stay for vertebral osteomyelitis
caused by MSSA — cefazolin IV q8h, planned 6-week total course.
Patient is hemodynamically stable, afebrile, ambulatory, has reliable
IV access (PICC line placed), home support, and proximity to ED for
urgent issues. Stewardship move: enroll in OPAT (outpatient parenteral
antimicrobial therapy) program for the remaining 4 weeks. Eligibility
criteria (IDSA 2018 OPAT guideline): (1) clinical stability — afebrile,
no hemodynamic instability, no need for daily ICU-level monitoring;
(2) reliable venous access — PICC, midline, or tunneled central line;
(3) drug compatibility — cefazolin q8h via 24-hour elastomeric pump,
OR ceftriaxone q24h short infusion (preferred for once-daily
simplicity), OR daptomycin q24h for MRSA, OR ertapenem q24h for ESBL;
(4) social support and patient capability for self-administration
or home health visits; (5) baseline labs (CBC, BMP, LFTs, drug levels
for vancomycin/aminoglycoside) plus weekly monitoring; (6) clear
communication channel — OPAT pharmacist, infectious disease specialist,
24-hour ER access. For this MSSA osteomyelitis case, switch from
cefazolin to ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily (ceftriaxone has slightly
lower MSSA cidal activity than cefazolin per Bai 2015 meta but is
easier for once-daily home infusion; cefazolin alternative is 2 g
IV q8h with elastomeric pump). Avoid: OPAT for unstable patients,
those without IV access plan, those with prior history of line-related
bacteremia, or those unable to perform line care. Next decision:
weekly clinical/lab monitoring (CBC, BMP, ESR/CRP trend), monthly
MRI for osteomyelitis at 3 months for treatment-response assessment,
transition to oral linezolid or oral fluoroquinolone for the final
2 weeks if MSSA susceptible.

Stewardship case: 5-day amoxicillin for community-acquired pneumonia outpatient — Spellberg 2018 short-course
response:
52-year-old healthy outpatient with cough, low-grade fever, focal
crackles right lower lobe, normal RR, normal SaO2, no comorbidities,
CURB-65 score 0. Diagnosed CAP, no admission needed. Pathogens by
probability: S. pneumoniae, atypicals (M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae,
Legionella), Hemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis. Standard
ATS-IDSA 2019 outpatient regimen for healthy adult: amoxicillin 1 g
PO TID x 5 days OR doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 5 days OR macrolide
(only if local pneumococcal macrolide resistance below 25 percent —
typically not in 2024 USA). Stewardship move: 5-day amoxicillin (or
doxycycline if penicillin-allergic). Rationale: ATS-IDSA 2019
shortened CAP duration to 5 days for clinically stable patients with
no signs of slow response (afebrile within 48 to 72 hours, no
respiratory deterioration). Spellberg 2018 review and earlier CAP-IT
pediatric trial supported short-course non-inferiority. The previous
"complete the bottle" 7- to 10-day courses were not evidence-based.
Stewardship benefit: less antibiotic exposure, less C. difficile risk,
less S. pneumoniae macrolide selection, lower cost. Avoid: empirical
respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) in healthy
outpatients — reserves these for inpatient or higher-risk; FQ-related
tendinopathy and aortic dissection black-box; FQ-related selection
pressure for resistance. Avoid: dual-coverage atypical + beta-lactam
in healthy outpatient (single-agent works for most). Next decision:
48 to 72 hour reassessment — clinical improvement (defervescence,
resolved hypoxia, eating); if not improving, switch class (e.g.
doxycycline added) and consider chest imaging for complications
(parapneumonic effusion, empyema).

Stewardship case: Probiotics or specific Lactobacillus rhamnosus for prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhea
response:
ICU patient on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam
then meropenem then ceftaz-avi over 6 weeks of complicated abdominal
infection); attending team asks about probiotics for diarrhea prevention.
Evidence: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Saccharomyces boulardii have
reduced antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) and C. difficile-associated
diarrhea (CDAD) in some meta-analyses (Goldenberg 2013 Cochrane showed
RR 0.40 for CDAD with probiotics; PLACIDE 2013 Lancet showed no
benefit in elderly hospitalized patients). Stewardship position:

Stewardship case: Antibiotic time-out at 72 hours — empirical-to-targeted assessment
response:
Surgical ICU patient day 4 post-laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis;
empirical regimen: piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin, fluconazole
(broad-spectrum + MRSA + Candida coverage given fecal peritonitis).
Day 3 — patient stable, afebrile, cultures growing E. coli ESBL-negative
sensitive to ceftriaxone, blood cultures negative, sterile peritoneal
fluid post-day-2, MRSA nasal PCR negative, no Candida growth.
Stewardship move: 72-hour antibiotic time-out (a CDC-endorsed and
IDSA-supported stewardship intervention, Fishman 2014). De-escalate
to: ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily plus metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h (or
simply ceftriaxone for non-anaerobic source if peritoneum sterile);
stop vancomycin (MRSA negative); stop fluconazole (no Candida growth).
Rationale: empirical broad-spectrum coverage at admission for fecal
peritonitis is appropriate; continued broad coverage at day 3 to 4
with culture-guided narrow option available is wasteful and
collateral-harming. SHARP, MRSA SBAR, and antibiotic-stewardship-
program audits show the 72-hour reassessment is one of the highest-
yield interventions for reducing inappropriate antibiotic days
(relative reduction 20 to 30 percent). Specific examples from RCT:
stopping vancomycin in MRSA-PCR-negative HAP saves 30 percent of
vanco days; stopping echinocandin if no fungal source identified
saves significant cost and fluconazole-R selection. Avoid: continuing
"just because patient is sick"; continuing because resident is
uncomfortable narrowing; multi-agent regimens beyond 72 hours
without source-specific rationale. Next decision: complete 4 to 7
day total course of narrowed regimen (4 days for source-controlled
intra-abdominal infection per STOP-IT trial, Sawyer 2015 NEJM —
4 days non-inferior to 8 days when source control achieved);
reassess at end of treatment for clinical cure.

Pathogen: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB)
response:
Resistance landscape: chromosomal blaOXA-51-like in all A. baumannii
provides intrinsic carbapenem hydrolysis; resistance becomes clinically
significant when blaOXA-51 is overexpressed (insertion sequence ISAba1
upstream) or when acquired blaOXA-23, blaOXA-24/40, blaOXA-58, blaOXA-72
(also class D carbapenemases) are present; some strains carry NDM-1
additionally; AdeABC efflux pump overexpression contributes; and PBP2
mutations alter target affinity. The result: carbapenem MIC greater
than 8 ug/mL, often greater than 32, with resistance to ALL
beta-lactams except sometimes sulbactam (which has intrinsic affinity
for PBP1 and PBP3 of Acinetobacter). First-line: high-dose ampicillin-
sulbactam 9 g IV q8h (sulbactam component is the active arm; high doses
drive sulbactam levels above MIC for many CRAB strains) PLUS minocycline
100 mg IV q12h or polymyxin-B 1.5 mg/kg q12h, with combination therapy
preferred over monotherapy in observational cohorts. NEW first-line
option: sulbactam-durlobactam 1 g + 1 g IV q6h — durlobactam DBO
inhibitor protects sulbactam from OXA-23 hydrolysis, restoring MIC50
to 1 to 2 ug/mL (Bouza 2023). Cefiderocol active in vitro but
CREDIBLE-CR trial showed numerically higher mortality vs best-available
therapy (FDA black-box concern). Tigecycline at high dose (100 mg IV
q12h) for non-bacteremic indications. Clinical syndromes: ventilator-
associated pneumonia (VAP, dominant ICU infection), bloodstream from
central lines, surgical-site after trauma or cardiothoracic surgery,
meningitis post-neurosurgery, wound colonization. Diagnostics: rapid
MALDI-TOF speciation; carbapenemase phenotypic (Carba NP, eCIM)
and molecular (blaOXA-23, blaOXA-24, blaNDM PCR); MIC for all
sulbactam-, polymyxin-, minocycline-, cefiderocol-based options.
Stewardship/IC: contact precautions, environmental disinfection
(Acinetobacter survives weeks on surfaces; bleach or hydrogen peroxide
vapor preferred for terminal cleaning), cohorting, and outbreak
investigation when greater than 3 cases/month per ward.

Pathogen: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
response:
Intrinsic resistance: chromosomal class B L1 metallo-beta-lactamase
(Zn-dependent, hydrolyzes carbapenems including meropenem and
imipenem) PLUS chromosomal class A L2 cephalosporinase (hydrolyzes
penicillins and most cephalosporins including ceftazidime); chromosomal
aac(6prime)-Iz (aminoglycoside acetyltransferase, knocks out gentamicin/
tobramycin/amikacin); SmeABC and SmeDEF efflux pumps. The combined
defenses make Stenotrophomonas intrinsically resistant to nearly all
beta-lactams and aminoglycosides — a "naturally pan-resistant"
organism. First-line: TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) 15
mg/kg/day TMP component IV divided q6 to 8h; TMP MIC50 0.06 to 0.5
ug/mL — bactericidal sequential folate-pathway blockade. Second-line:
levofloxacin 750 mg IV/PO q24h (resistance ~30 percent in some
regions, especially CF cohorts); minocycline 200 mg IV/PO load then
100 mg q12h; tigecycline (variable activity, CMS Cmax ceiling
problem); cefiderocol (active via Trojan-horse uptake bypassing L1
MBL hydrolysis); chloramphenicol (rarely used, gray-baby and aplastic
anemia risk). Clinical syndromes: nosocomial pneumonia (especially
ventilator-associated and CF-associated), bloodstream from central
lines, wound and skin/soft-tissue, urinary tract (rarely community,
mostly hospital-acquired catheter-associated). High mortality in
bacteremia (~30 percent). Diagnostics: MALDI-TOF; routine antimicrobial
susceptibility for TMP-SMX, levo, minocycline, ceftazidime (still
L2-hydrolyzed but check); Etest for moxifloxacin; molecular BLNAR-
like detection not standard. Stewardship/IC: contact precautions
because environmental survival; common in water sources (sink drains,
ventilator humidifiers — outbreak source investigation matters);
prefer source control (line removal) when bacteremia from CVC.
Combination therapy (TMP-SMX + levofloxacin or TMP-SMX + minocycline)
considered for severe pneumonia or persistent bacteremia.

Pathogen: Burkholderia cepacia complex
response:
Resistance landscape: complex of 20+ species including B. cepacia,
B. cenocepacia, B. multivorans, B. dolosa, B. vietnamiensis, B. anthina.
Intrinsic resistance: chromosomal class A AmpC-like (PenA) cephalosporinase,
class B carbapenemase (variable presence — KPC-like activity in some
strains), AmrAB-OprA and AmrAB-OprM efflux pumps, polymyxin resistance
via lipid-A modification (4-amino-4-deoxy-arabinose, similar to mcr
mechanism), and target-mediated changes including PBP3 modifications.
The combined defenses give intrinsic resistance to ALL aminoglycosides,
polymyxin/colistin, and most beta-lactams. First-line: TMP-SMX
(sequential folate blockade — same as for Stenotrophomonas), 5 mg/kg
TMP component q12h; second-line: meropenem 2 g IV q8h with extended
infusion (penetrates despite chromosomal carbapenemase in some strains),
ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h (variable susceptibility — test specifically),
chloramphenicol (limited use), minocycline. Combination therapy is
common in severe disease (TMP-SMX + meropenem, or TMP-SMX +
ceftazidime) for cystic fibrosis pulmonary exacerbation. Clinical
syndromes: chronic CF lung infection (B. cenocepacia is the most
virulent species and CONTRAINDICATES lung transplantation in many
programs because of high post-transplant mortality from B. cenocepacia
sepsis); pneumonia in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) patients
(a defining infection); bloodstream from CVC contamination
(water-source outbreaks); rare community pneumonia. Diagnostics:
species-level identification by MALDI-TOF or recA gene sequencing
(clinically important because B. cenocepacia carries lung-transplant
contraindication while B. multivorans does not); susceptibility
testing per CLSI Burkholderia-specific. Stewardship/IC: strict
contact precautions in CF clinics, water-system surveillance for
Burkholderia in hospital water sources, segregation of CF patients
with B. cenocepacia from those without to prevent cross-transmission.

Pathogen: Mycobacterium abscessus complex
response:
Resistance landscape: rapidly-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium
with three subspecies (M. abscessus subsp. abscessus, M. massiliense,
M. bolletii). Intrinsic resistance: chromosomal blaMab class A
beta-lactamase hydrolyzes most beta-lactams; erm(41) gene confers
inducible macrolide resistance — but only in subsp. abscessus and
subsp. bolletii (subsp. massiliense has truncated erm(41) and remains
macrolide-susceptible, important for therapy choice and prognosis);
chromosomal mph efflux limits clinical drug levels; cell-wall mycolic
acid layer reduces drug penetration. The combined defenses make
M. abscessus complex among the most drug-resistant pathogens treated.
First-line (intensive phase, 4 to 6 weeks IV): amikacin 15 mg/kg IV
q24h PLUS imipenem 1 g IV q6h or cefoxitin 12 g/day IV PLUS azithromycin
500 mg PO daily (only if subsp. massiliense or erm(41) inactive subsp.
abscessus). Continuation phase (12 to 24 months oral): azithromycin +
clofazimine + linezolid + bedaquiline + tigecycline combinations
individualized. Clinical syndromes: chronic pulmonary infection
(especially in cystic fibrosis, structural lung disease,
bronchiectasis), skin/soft-tissue from contaminated water/aesthetic
procedures (tattoo, facial rejuvenation, breast implant, plastic
surgery), disseminated in immunocompromised. Diagnostics: AFB smear
and culture (rapidly growing, around 7 days vs M. tuberculosis 2 to
6 weeks); MALDI-TOF speciation; molecular subspecies identification
by hsp65 sequencing or rpoB sequencing; erm(41) genotype crucial
for prognosis (massiliense vs abscessus); susceptibility for amikacin,
imipenem, cefoxitin, doxycycline, linezolid, clarithromycin (with
14-day incubation to detect inducible resistance). Stewardship/IC:
no person-to-person transmission for most cases (water/environmental
source); CF-specific transmissible clones with hyper-virulence
(M. abscessus DCC1, DCC2) monitored at CF centers; infection control
around water sources at risk-prone facilities (humidifiers, cosmetic
injection setups).

Pathogen: Multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MDR-TB)
response:
Resistance landscape: defined as resistance to at least both rifampin
AND isoniazid (the two most active first-line drugs); extensively
drug-resistant (XDR) adds resistance to a fluoroquinolone AND a
second-line injectable (amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin) or
bedaquiline/linezolid. Mutations: rpoB (rifampin), katG Ser315Thr
and inhA promoter (isoniazid), gyrA S91P/D94G (fluoroquinolones),
rrs A1401G (amikacin), atpE D28V (bedaquiline), 23S rRNA G2576T
(linezolid). Global epidemiology: ~410,000 incident MDR-TB cases

Pathogen: Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus
response:
Resistance landscape: Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common cause
of invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised hosts (hematologic
malignancy, stem cell transplant, solid organ transplant, COVID-
associated). Azole resistance arises by two main pathways: (1)
patient-driven — emerges during long-term azole therapy in single
patients, with cyp51A point mutations (G54E/V/W, G138C, M220I);
(2) environment-driven — through agricultural azole use selecting
strains with cyp51A tandem-repeat promoter mutations (TR34/L98H and
TR46/Y121F/T289A), found globally and patients can present at first
diagnosis with already-resistant strains. The TR34/L98H mutation
raises voriconazole MIC from 0.5 to 4 to 8 (resistant); TR46/Y121F/T289A
raises voriconazole specifically while sparing posaconazole partially.

liposomal amphotericin-B 3 to 5 mg/kg IV q24h OR isavuconazole 200 mg
PO/IV q8h x 6 doses load then daily (active against TR34/L98H but
cross-resistance with TR46 — check MIC). Combination therapy
(voriconazole + echinocandin like caspofungin) considered in severe
cases despite mixed evidence (Marr 2015). Clinical syndromes: invasive
pulmonary aspergillosis (cavitary nodules, halo sign, air-crescent
sign on CT), tracheobronchial in lung-transplant, CNS (rare,

percent in hematologic malignancy, false positives with piperacillin-

specific; serum/BAL Aspergillus PCR; cyp51A genotype on positive
isolate; serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan (non-specific, also positive for

essential during therapy (target trough 1 to 5.5 voriconazole, greater
than 1.25 posaconazole). Stewardship/IC: HEPA-filtered rooms for
high-risk neutropenic patients; primary prophylaxis with posaconazole
DR-tab during AML induction or post-transplant; surveillance
galactomannan twice-weekly during high-risk neutropenia.

Pathogen: Candida auris
response:
Resistance landscape: emerging multidrug-resistant yeast first reported
2009 (Japan), now endemic in over 50 countries. Five geographic clades
(I South Asia, II East Asia, III Africa, IV South America, V Iran)
with differing resistance profiles. Around 90 percent of clinical
isolates are fluconazole-resistant (intrinsic-like, ERG11 mutations
Y132F and K143R analogous to C. albicans azole-R), 30 to 50 percent
echinocandin-resistant (FKS1 hot-spot S639P/F mutations emerging in
cohorts with prior echinocandin pressure), 30 percent amphotericin-
resistant (mechanism not fully understood, possibly ergosterol
membrane modification). First-line: echinocandin (caspofungin 70 mg
load then 50 mg q24h, or micafungin 100 mg q24h, or anidulafungin 200
mg load then 100 mg q24h) until susceptibility known. If echinocandin-
resistant, lipid-formulation amphotericin B 3 to 5 mg/kg q24h;
susceptibility testing essential for every isolate because clade-
based prediction is unreliable. Combination therapy (echinocandin +
amphotericin) sometimes used for breakthrough or persistent fungemia.
Clinical syndromes: bloodstream (catheter-associated, post-surgical),
wound colonization, urinary, ear infection (notably the original
"auris" naming from Japanese ear discharge isolates); high mortality
around 30 to 50 percent in candidemia. Diagnostics: MALDI-TOF
identification (note: requires updated database — older databases
misidentify as C. haemulonii); molecular ITS or D1/D2 sequencing
confirms species; FKS1 sequencing for echinocandin resistance;
ERG11 sequencing for azole resistance. Stewardship/IC: STRICT
contact precautions and environmental controls — C. auris persists
on surfaces for weeks, resists routine quaternary-ammonium
disinfectants (EPA List P or List K disinfectants required:
chlorine bleach, hydrogen peroxide); cohorting; surveillance
cultures for new admissions in high-prevalence regions; outbreak
response with public-health partnership; CDC and WHO notification
required for new clusters.

Pathogen: Cryptococcus neoformans var. grubii (HIV/AIDS-associated cryptococcal meningitis)
response:
Resistance landscape: traditionally susceptible to amphotericin and
flucytosine; fluconazole resistance emerging in some African cohorts
with prolonged exposure (azole pressure, ERG11 mutations). Encapsulated
yeast — the polysaccharide capsule (glucuronoxylomannan, GXM) is the
virulence factor and a diagnostic target. Pathophysiology: inhalation
from environmental source (pigeon guano, soil); pulmonary primary
infection often subclinical; hematogenous dissemination to CNS in
immunocompromised (CD4 less than 100 in HIV/AIDS — the classic host
condition). First-line for cryptococcal meningoencephalitis: induction
with liposomal amphotericin B 3 to 4 mg/kg IV q24h PLUS flucytosine
25 mg/kg PO q6h x 2 weeks (van der Horst 1997 NEJM established
synergy); consolidation with fluconazole 800 mg PO daily x 8 weeks;
maintenance with fluconazole 200 mg daily x 6 to 12 months minimum
(or until CD4 greater than 200 sustained). Clinical syndromes:
meningoencephalitis (most common), pulmonary cryptococcosis, skin
lesions (umbilicated papules), osteoarticular, prostatitis. Subacute
meningitis with headache, low-grade fever, meningismus, and elevated
ICP (often greater than 25 cm H2O — one of the diagnostic and
management challenges). Diagnostics: serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg)
lateral-flow assay (sensitivity greater than 99 percent and specificity
around 97 percent in HIV); CSF CrAg and India ink; LP with opening
pressure measurement (high pressure requires repeat LPs or shunt);
culture; quantitative CrAg titers track therapy response. Stewardship/IC:
no person-to-person transmission; pre-emptive screening with serum
CrAg in HIV-positive patients with CD4 less than 200 (or less than 100)
at ART initiation reduces incident meningitis (REMSTART, ACTG A5277);
ICP management with daily LPs to drain CSF until OP normalizes;
avoid steroids (no benefit, may worsen) — different from TB
meningitis where steroids help.

Pathogen: Pneumocystis jirovecii
response:
Resistance landscape: opportunistic fungus (formerly classified as
protozoan); cannot be cultured. Resistance emerges via mutations in
DHPS (dihydropteroate synthase, target of sulfa drugs) — codon 55
and 57 mutations (Thr55Ala, Pro57Ser) raise sulfa MIC; clinically
relevant in regions with high prophylaxis use, with reported prevalence
5 to 30 percent of clinical isolates; clinical impact debated (some
studies show worse outcomes, others not). Atovaquone resistance
via cytochrome b mutations also reported. First-line treatment:
TMP-SMX 15 to 20 mg/kg/day TMP component IV/PO divided q6 to 8h
for severe disease, or 2 DS tabs PO TID for mild-moderate, x 21
days. Add adjunctive corticosteroids (prednisone 40 mg BID x 5 days,
then taper over 21 days) for moderate-severe PCP — defined as
PaO2 less than 70 mmHg or A-a gradient greater than 35 — Bozzette
1990 NEJM and CSCAP cohort showed mortality reduction. Alternative
regimens for sulfa-allergy or treatment failure: pentamidine 4 mg/kg
IV daily (toxic — pancreatitis, hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia, AKI,
QTc); clindamycin 600 to 900 mg IV q6h PLUS primaquine 30 mg PO
daily (alternative for moderate disease); atovaquone 750 mg PO BID
with food (mild disease only); dapsone PLUS trimethoprim. Clinical
syndromes: subacute pneumonia in HIV/AIDS (CD4 less than 200) —
nonproductive cough, exertional dyspnea, hypoxemia, ground-glass on
CT; in non-HIV immunocompromised (steroid-dependent connective tissue
disease, transplant, hematologic malignancy on chemotherapy) the
presentation is often more abrupt and severe. Diagnostics: induced
sputum or BAL with Giemsa or methenamine silver staining; PCP PCR
(highly sensitive, distinguishes infection from colonization with
quantitative PCR copies); BAL beta-D-glucan greater than 80 pg/mL;
LDH elevated. Stewardship/IC: primary prophylaxis with TMP-SMX 1
DS daily (or 1 DS three times weekly) for HIV-positive with CD4 less
than 200, post-allogeneic-transplant for at least 6 months,
steroid-dependent rheumatologic patients on prednisone greater than
20 mg daily for over 4 weeks; alternatives for sulfa-allergy:
dapsone (after G6PD screen), atovaquone, aerosolized pentamidine.

Pathogen: Toxoplasma gondii (cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV/AIDS)
response:
Resistance landscape: protozoan parasite (apicomplexan); resistance
uncommon in clinical practice but emerging via DHFR mutations
(analogous to TMP-resistance) and DHPS mutations under sulfa
pressure. Standard regimens have remained effective since 1980s.
First-line for cerebral toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine 200 mg PO load
then 50 to 75 mg PO daily PLUS sulfadiazine 1 to 1.5 g PO QID PLUS
leucovorin (folinic acid) 10 to 20 mg PO daily (to prevent
pyrimethamine-induced bone marrow suppression by replacing reduced
folate that bypasses pyrimethamine-blocked DHFR); duration 6 weeks
acute, then chronic suppression at half-dose until immune
reconstitution. Alternative for sulfa allergy: pyrimethamine PLUS
clindamycin 600 mg PO q6h PLUS leucovorin (the IDSA-preferred
alternative); pyrimethamine PLUS atovaquone PLUS leucovorin
(alternative-alternative); TMP-SMX (15 mg/kg/day TMP component) is
a single-drug alternative with similar efficacy in some studies
(Schmidt 2006). Clinical syndromes: cerebral toxoplasmosis in
HIV/AIDS (CD4 less than 100, classic ring-enhancing lesions on MRI,
usually multiple, basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction
preference); chorioretinitis (acute or congenital); congenital
toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial
calcifications in newborn); reactivated disease in transplant
recipients (heart transplant especially — donor-derived if seropositive
donor to seronegative recipient). Diagnostics: serum Toxoplasma IgG
(positive in chronic latent infection, present in 20 to 50 percent
of US adults); serum IgM (acute or recent); MRI brain (multiple
ring-enhancing lesions, basal ganglia preference); CSF PCR for
Toxoplasma DNA (in high-risk HIV patient, distinguishes from
lymphoma — though brain biopsy may be needed if empirical therapy
fails by 2 weeks). Empirical therapy in HIV with seropositive
Toxoplasma IgG and ring-enhancing lesions reasonable; lack of
response by 2 weeks → biopsy for primary CNS lymphoma vs Toxo.
Stewardship/IC: primary prophylaxis with TMP-SMX 1 DS daily
(also covers PCP) in HIV patients with CD4 less than 100 AND
Toxoplasma IgG positive; discontinue when CD4 greater than 200
sustained for 6 months on ART.

Drug: Daptomycin
response:
Cyclic lipopeptide of 13 amino acids with an n-decanoyl (C10) fatty acid tail
attached to the N-terminal tryptophan. Ten of the residues form the macrocycle
via an ester bond between Thr4 and Kyn13 (kynurenine, an unusual non-canonical

Drug: Linezolid

in serotonin).

Drug: Rifampin
response:
Semi-synthetic rifamycin (parent natural product rifamycin SV from
Amycolatopsis mediterranei). Chemistry: ansa-bridged naphthoquinone with
a C3 aliphatic chain, C8 hydroxyl, C21/C23 hydroxyls coordinating water
molecules. The 4-methylpiperazine substitution at C3 distinguishes
rifampin from rifabutin and rifapentine. Mechanism: binds the
bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (DDRP) beta-subunit (rpoB) at
a specific channel near the catalytic Mg2+ that lies between the
DNA template and the nascent RNA strand. Rifampin physically blocks
RNA chain extension once the nascent RNA reaches 2 to 3 nucleotides,
preventing transcription elongation. Selectivity: human RNA polymerase
II/III have different beta-subunit architecture, do not bind rifampin.
Spectrum: highly active against M. tuberculosis (MIC 0.06 ug/mL),
M. leprae, all staphylococci including MRSA (MIC 0.008 to 0.06),
streptococci, neisseria, Legionella, and intracellular pathogens
(Brucella, Bartonella). Outer-membrane diffusion limits gram-negative
activity in many strains. Resistance: rpoB point mutations (typically
Ser531Leu, His526Tyr, Asp516Val in M. tuberculosis numbering — the
"Rifampin Resistance Determining Region" RRDR of 81 bp) emerge at
frequency around 10^-7 to 10^-8 per replication. Single-step
resistance is the reason rifampin is NEVER used as monotherapy for
active infection (only for prophylaxis or single-dose treatment of
asymptomatic colonization like meningococcal contact prophylaxis).
PK/PD: AUC/MIC about 65 for stasis. Standard 600 mg PO daily
(or 10 mg/kg) achieves AUC of 50 to 100 mg.h/L, hitting target.
100 percent oral bioavailability when fasted (food reduces by 30
percent). Tox: orange-red discoloration of body fluids (urine, tears,
sweat, contact lens staining — cosmetic, counsel patient); hepatic
enzyme rise (around 14 percent), severe hepatitis 1 percent;
flu-like syndrome with intermittent dosing; thrombocytopenia, hemolytic
anemia, AKI (rare). CRITICAL: potent CYP3A4/2C9/2C19 inducer —
reduces warfarin INR (re-titrate), oral contraceptive failure
(contraception backup needed), HIV protease inhibitor levels (HAART
failure), tacrolimus and cyclosporine reduction in transplant
(rejection risk). The drug interaction profile is the practical
limit on rifampin use.

Drug: Trimethoprim
response:
Synthetic 2,4-diaminopyrimidine, structural analog of dihydrofolate.
Chemistry: 2,4-diaminopyrimidine ring (the substrate-mimicking head)
linked via a methylene bridge to a 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl ring (the
hydrophobic anchor). The 2,4-diamino group hydrogen-bonds with bacterial
DHFR active-site residues (Glu30, Asp27 in E. coli numbering),
mimicking the hydrogen-bond pattern of dihydrofolate's pteridine ring.
Mechanism: competitively inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase
(DHFR), the enzyme that reduces dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate
using NADPH. Tetrahydrofolate is the universal carrier of
one-carbon units for thymidine, purine, methionine, and serine
synthesis; blocking DHFR halts thymidine production and stops DNA
replication. Selectivity: bacterial DHFR has different active-site
geometry than mammalian DHFR — trimethoprim has 60,000-fold higher
affinity for bacterial DHFR than human DHFR. Single-agent action is
bacteriostatic; combined with sulfamethoxazole (which blocks the
preceding DHPS step) becomes bactericidal via sequential pathway
blockade. Spectrum: broad — most Enterobacterales, S. aureus
(community MRSA), Stenotrophomonas, Burkholderia, Listeria, PCP,
Toxoplasma, Nocardia. Resistance: chromosomal DHFR mutations
(rarely clinically significant), or acquired dfrA17, dfrA1, dfrB
gene cassettes encoding plasmid-borne DHFR variants with reduced
TMP affinity (Ki 1000-fold higher), often in class 1 integrons
alongside sul1 (sulfonamide R), aac(6prime)-Ib-cr, and qnr. PK/PD:
AUC/MIC about 80 for combined TMP-SMX activity. Standard dose 160/800
mg PO BID (DS tab); 5 to 20 mg/kg/day TMP component IV for severe.
Tox: hyperkalemia (TMP blocks ENaC sodium channel in distal tubule,
same mechanism as amiloride), bone marrow suppression (folate-pathway
collateral on host hematopoiesis — give leucovorin if cytopenia),
hepatic enzyme rise, sulfa hypersensitivity (SJS/TEN at HLA-B*15:02
and B*58:01), nephrolithiasis (sulfamethoxazole crystallization).
Combination of TMP + sulfa is one of the most-used antibacterials
globally because of broad spectrum, oral availability, low cost.

Drug: Metronidazole
response:
Nitroimidazole prodrug requiring intracellular reduction. Chemistry:
2-methyl-5-nitroimidazole-1-ethanol — small polar molecule with
excellent tissue and CSF penetration. The 5-nitro group is the
pharmacophore. Mechanism: anaerobic bacteria (and some protozoa)
have low-redox-potential ferredoxin or pyruvate-ferredoxin
oxidoreductase (PFOR) that donates electrons to the 5-nitro group,
reducing it to a nitroso radical anion, then a hydroxylamine, then
reactive intermediates that covalently bind to bacterial DNA. The
reduced metronidazole forms DNA strand breaks and adducts,
triggering bactericidal kill. Aerobic bacteria and host cells
cannot reduce nitroimidazoles efficiently (their redox potential is
too high), giving anaerobic-selective toxicity. Spectrum: anaerobic
gram-negatives (Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella, Fusobacterium,
Porphyromonas), anaerobic gram-positives (Clostridium including
C. difficile and C. perfringens, Peptostreptococcus); inactive
against aerobic bacteria; protozoa (Giardia, Trichomonas, Entamoeba
histolytica); microaerophilic Helicobacter pylori. MIC50: B. fragilis
0.5 to 4, C. difficile 0.5 to 2, Giardia 1, T. vaginalis 0.5.
Resistance: nimA-J genes (nim operon) encode nitroimidazole reductase
that converts 5-nitro to 5-amino — inactive form, prevents activation.
C. difficile metronidazole resistance is rising (now ~5 to 15 percent
in some surveillance), driving the IDSA-SHEA 2021 downgrade of
metronidazole from first-line to alternative-only for non-severe CDI.
PK/PD: AUC/MIC about 70. 500 mg PO/IV q8h; oral bioavailability
around 100 percent. Tox: metallic taste (universal), GI upset,
peripheral neuropathy at cumulative doses greater than 30 g (limits
total course length), disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (avoid
ethanol during therapy and 48 hours after), seizures at high IV
doses or in elderly, optic neuritis (rare), pancreatitis (rare).
Carcinogenicity in rodents from high-dose chronic exposure (clinical
relevance debated; FDA Pregnancy Category B but counsel during
first-trimester use).

Drug: Amphotericin B
response:
Polyene macrolide of 38-membered ring with seven conjugated double bonds
(the heptaene chromophore), an amino-glycoside-like mycosamine sugar at
C19, and a C13 carboxylic acid. Mechanism: amphotericin inserts into
ergosterol-rich fungal membranes, with eight molecules forming a
transmembrane "barrel" pore lined by the polar hydroxylated face of each
molecule and surrounded by ergosterol. The pore allows leak of K+, Mg2+,
ATP, and small molecules out of the fungal cell, leading to depolarization
and cell death. Selectivity: ergosterol is the main fungal sterol but
cholesterol (the human sterol) also binds amphotericin with about
10-fold lower affinity — this cross-reactivity drives mammalian
cell toxicity, especially in renal tubular cells and red blood cells.
Lipid formulations (liposomal AmphoB, AmBisome; AmphoB lipid complex,
Abelcet; AmphoB cholesteryl sulfate complex, Amphotec) reduce mammalian
affinity by sequestering AmphoB in lipid carriers that release drug
preferentially at fungal infection sites with elevated lipase activity,
cutting nephrotoxicity from 25 to 30 percent (deoxycholate AmphoB) to
5 to 10 percent (liposomal). Spectrum: nearly universal antifungal —
Candida (most species), Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Mucorales (Rhizopus,
Mucor), endemic fungi (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides), some
protozoa (Leishmania donovani — visceral leishmaniasis treatment).
MIC: Candida albicans 0.25 to 1 ug/mL, Aspergillus 1 to 2, Cryptococcus
0.25 to 1. Resistance: rare; some Candida lusitaniae and C. terreus
have intrinsic resistance via altered ergosterol biosynthesis (ERG3
pathway changes producing alternative sterols that AmphoB does not
bind well). PK/PD: AUC0-24/MIC about 10 for fungistatic activity.
Liposomal AmphoB 3 to 5 mg/kg IV q24h; Cmax 30 to 50 ug/mL. Tox:
infusion-reaction (rigors, fever, hypotension — premedicate with
acetaminophen, diphenhydramine, hydrocortisone for severe);
nephrotoxicity (renal vasoconstriction + tubular injury), hypokalemia
and hypomagnesemia (renal wasting), normocytic anemia (erythropoietin
suppression and direct red-cell membrane toxicity), hepatic enzyme
rise. Liposomal forms are preferred for prolonged therapy, but cost
is 5 to 10-fold higher.

Drug: Mupirocin
response:
Pseudomonic acid A — natural product from Pseudomonas fluorescens.
Chemistry: 9-hydroxy-nonanoic acid epoxide ester linked to monic acid

synthetase (IleRS) at the active site, mimicking the natural substrate
